headline: High risk of capability conflict and cascading errors: ctx can observe Claude Code events while marketingskills writes shared skill files and uses shared context.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: ctx observes Claude Code PostToolUse and Stop events, so it can ingest another agent’s outputs; marketingskills explicitly says skills reference each other and build on shared context. That creates an instruction-smuggling path if shared files or event text contain attacker-controlled content. The exact bridge is not fully documented, so I choose medium over low.
conditions: IF ctx consumes Claude Code event text as instructions without provenance filtering
IF marketingskills writes skill content into shared files that ctx later parses
mitigations: Add a provenance tag to all cross-agent text before parsing
Restrict ctx to read-only observation of tool events
Separate the agents into different workspaces
Require explicit allowlists for instruction-bearing fields
requires-engineering: implement content-sanitization and provenance checks

B_data_leakage.rationale: Both profiles expose filesystem surfaces, and marketingskills writes skill/context files while ctx touches audit/runtime logs, graph data, and MCP servers. Even though ctx’s upload behavior is not explicit, the shared file-based workflow makes leakage of marketing content or logs plausible in default use. Uncertainty about the exact sharing boundary pushes this above low.
conditions: IF both agents operate in the same workspace directory
IF ctx records or forwards audit/runtime logs containing marketing content
mitigations: Use separate directories for each agent
Redact sensitive fields before handoff
Disable log sharing between agents
Review file permissions on shared folders
requires-engineering: add per-agent data-loss controls

C_capability_conflict.rationale: ctx supports multiple instances and has filesystem/file-oriented surfaces; marketingskills has read/write filesystem plus subprocess and allowlisted network egress. If both write to the same workspace or shared skill files, concurrent modification and state corruption are likely in default multi-instance use. The pair’s overlapping write surfaces make high severity appropriate.
conditions: IF both agents write to the same directory
IF multiple instances run concurrently without locking
mitigations: Assign separate output directories
Serialize writes with a lock file
Disable concurrent runs during edits
Use git branches per agent
requires-engineering: add optimistic concurrency control

D_cascading_error.rationale: marketingskills is designed to build on shared context, so it may treat ctx-produced context as authoritative; ctx in turn observes tool events and logs that can be reused downstream. That creates a plausible chain where one agent’s output becomes the other’s input without verification. The pathway exists, but there is no direct evidence of autonomous action-taking, so medium fits.
conditions: IF marketingskills consumes ctx-generated context without validation
IF ctx-derived summaries are reused as source material for marketing outputs
mitigations: Insert a human review step between agents
Mark ctx outputs as untrusted by default
Require citations for any reused facts
Compare outputs against source files before reuse
requires-engineering: add verification gates between agents

E_compliance.rationale: No residency, certification, or retention mismatch is documented in either profile. The only compliance-relevant clue is that ctx touches audit/runtime logs while marketingskills writes skill/context files, which could create retention concerns if combined, but the profiles do not show a concrete regulated-data flow. I therefore keep this low and cite both profiles for the logging/file surfaces.
conditions: IF regulated data is stored in ctx audit/runtime logs
IF marketingskills persists the same regulated data in shared skill files
mitigations: Avoid placing regulated data in shared files
Set short log-retention windows
Review file retention settings
Separate regulated and non-regulated workspaces
requires-engineering: document residency and retention policies
